title: The Hazelnut Block Pietro Ferrero Made When Cocoa Ran Short
dek: After a failed shop in Turin, an Alba pastry maker built a cheap sweet from the hazelnuts on his own hills, and it became the Ferrero company.

story.event: Making Pasta Gianduja (Giandujot), a sliceable hazelnut block, in Alba when cocoa was scarce, and founding the company
story.summary: With cocoa scarce and expensive during and after the Second World War, the Alba pastry maker Pietro Ferrero built a cheap product around local hazelnuts: Pasta Gianduja, or Giandujot, a foil-wrapped block of hazelnuts, sugar and a little cocoa sliced onto bread, sold at a fifth of the price of chocolate. It sold well, and Ferrero was registered as a company on 14 May 1946. Pietro died in 1949; his son Michele later turned the idea into Nutella.
paragraphs: Pietro Ferrero, born in 1898 in the Piedmont village of Farigliano, was a pastry maker who had already watched one business fail. According to Italy's AGI news agency, he opened a large pastry shop on via Sant'Anselmo in Turin; it did not last, and he went back to Alba, the hill town where he and his wife Piera had settled after their marriage. In 1942, by his company's own history, he opened a small workshop on via Rattazzi to experiment, while Piera ran their pastry shop on via Maestra.

The war made even simple ingredients hard to find. Cocoa was scarce and dear; hazelnuts, which grow across the hills around Alba, were plentiful and cheap. Ferrero built his product around the local crop: a block of hazelnuts, sugar and a little cocoa, wrapped in tinfoil, that could be cut into slices and laid on bread. He called it Pasta Gianduja, then Giandujot, after a Piedmontese carnival mask. A kilo cost 600 lire, against 3,000 for a kilo of chocolate. The company's history says his aim was to stop sweets being a luxury for the few or for feast days.

The substitute sold. When word went round Alba that the workshop wanted five or six workers, the company recalls, it was news in a town where the only other hiring just after the war was for a municipal street sweeper. Production in February 1946 was three quintals, about 300 kilograms; by the end of that year about fifty people worked there, and about a hundred the year after. On 14 May 1946 Ferrero was registered with the Chamber of Commerce, and a first factory went up on land Pietro had bought earlier on via Vivaro. His younger brother Giovanni built the sales network.

On 4 September 1948 a flood filled the factory with mud as it prepared for Christmas production; staff and the Ferrero brothers dug it out over four days, and it was running again by the end of the month. On 2 March 1949 Pietro died of a heart attack, aged 51. Piera, Giovanni and their son Michele carried the business on. A spreadable version, Supercrema, followed in the 1950s, and in 1964 the first jar of Nutella came off the line in Alba.

quote.text: The linen cap is that prescribed by the rules of ceremony, but now a silk one is worn. It is economical, and I follow the common practice.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius, strict about ceremony, accepted a cheaper material without fuss; in the very next verse he refuses a shortcut he calls arrogant. Ferrero's hazelnuts were a silk cap, not a skipped bow: a substitute that kept the purpose, something sweet on ordinary bread, while changing what it was made of.

reflection: Ferrero did not wait for cocoa to come back. He looked at what grew on the hills outside his workshop and asked what it could become, and he priced the result for people who could not afford chocolate. The constraint did not make the idea; it made the idea necessary.

Not every standard deserves to bend. Confucius kept bowing below the hall when everyone else had stopped. But some of what you are holding out for may be a linen cap: the proper version of a thing, when a humbler one would serve the same people just as well, and sooner.
invitation: Name one thing you are waiting for before you can begin a piece of work. Write down what you already have within reach that could stand in for it, even roughly, for one week.

cross_checks.claim: Cocoa was scarce and expensive in wartime and post-war Italy, and Ferrero used local hazelnuts to save on it.
Giandujot was a sliceable block sold far more cheaply than chocolate (600 against 3,000 lire a kilo).
Ferrero was incorporated on 14 May 1946 and had about fifty staff by the end of that year.
Pietro Ferrero died on 2 March 1949, and the first jar of Nutella was made in Alba in 1964.

research_notes: Production figures: the Ferrero history says production was three quintals in February 1946 and 'over a thousand' by the end of the year without repeating the unit; AGI gives the same numbers, which reads as over a thousand quintals (about 100 tonnes), while one summary read it as 1,000 kg. Because the unit is ambiguous, the story gives only the February figure and the staff numbers, on which both agree (about fifty by the end of 1946, about a hundred the next year). The AGI article closely follows the company's own history in places, so the AFP obituaries are used as the independent check on the cocoa shortage and the hazelnut substitution. AFP's two versions differ slightly: one says he added hazelnut to save money on chocolate, the other on cocoa 'in short supply after World War II'; the company says the war made even simple ingredients unobtainable. The failed Turin shop comes from AGI alone and is attributed to it; no source gives its dates. The Local (2024) says the product cost four to five times less than chocolate, consistent with 600 against 3,000 lire. Supercrema: The Local implies the rename; the company dates it only to the 1950s, which the story follows. The story does not use the popular tale of a summer heatwave melting the paste into a spread, which appears only on weak sites. Funding: no source mentions outside investors; 'bootstrapped' reflects a family workshop growing out of its own pastry shop, and is an inference. The Confucius verse is about ceremonial dress; the connection applies it by analogy and refers to the next verse (IX.3.2) on bowing below the hall.
